COST06-BP02 Select resource type, size, and number based on data
Base the type, size, and number of resources on evidence of the
    workload's compute, memory, throughput, and storage demands. Draw
    that evidence from a prior version of the workload, vendor
    documentation, published benchmarks, or a cost model.
Desired outcome:
You size resources from measured or documented workload
        characteristics rather than estimates.
Your sizing decisions account for multiple dimensions, including
        compute, memory, storage, and network, not a single dimension.
You match workloads to purpose-built resource types when the
        workload profile justifies them.
Your resource selections trace back to a named data source that
        another engineer can review.
Common anti-patterns:
Allocating resources from unsubstantiated estimates.
Sizing on a single characteristic, such as CPU, while ignoring
        memory, storage, or network.
Choosing the largest available resource to avoid any risk of
        under-provisioning.
Reusing a resource type from an unrelated workload because it is
        familiar.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Workloads perform well under load without paying for capacity
        they do not use.
Sizing decisions are defensible because they rest on documented
        evidence.
Purpose-built resource types deliver better price performance
        than general-purpose equivalents for the workloads that fit
        them.
Multi-dimensional analysis helps prevent a single overlooked
        requirement from causing a bottleneck.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
Medium
Implementation guidance
A workload's profile spans compute, memory, storage, throughput,
      and network demands. Match resources to that profile without
      excess. The profile is rarely obvious before the workload runs, so
      without data, sizing tends toward the largest option.
Sizing on one visible dimension, such as high CPU, can miss the
      dimension that actually constrains the workload, such as memory.
      Resource families each target a different bottleneck: general
      purpose, compute optimized, memory optimized, storage optimized,
      and accelerated. To select the family, first identify the
      constraining dimension by evaluating all dimensions together.
The strongest evidence comes from a prior version of the workload,
      whether on-premises or in another environment, because it reflects
      real behavior. Without one, vendor documentation and published
      benchmarks provide a starting point. A cost model from earlier
      analysis maps expected usage to specific resource dimensions. With
      weaker sources, choose more conservatively and validate against
      real measurements sooner.
Many processor and instance types target specific workload shapes,
      such as machine learning training, high-throughput storage, or
      particular instruction sets. They deliver better price performance
      than general-purpose resources for those workloads. The cost is
      reduced flexibility, a purpose-built resource that no longer
      matches the workload is harder to repurpose. Prefer specialized
      options for stable, well-understood profiles. Keep general purpose
      when the profile is uncertain or changing.
Serverless and managed components expose fewer sizing knobs, and
      those knobs still drive cost.
AWS Lambda
cost scales with allocated memory. Test to find the
      best cost-performance setting. If a prior version of the function
      is already running,
AWS Compute Optimizer
recommends a memory size, narrowing the
      range to test.
AWS Graviton
(Arm) processors lower cost for the same work on
      Lambda, AWS Fargate, and many instance families where your runtime
      supports Arm.
This best practice covers initial resource selection from data. To
      keep resources correctly sized as demand changes, see
COST06-BP03 Select resource type, size, and number automatically based on metrics
. For
      each resource family's characteristics and use cases, see the
Amazon EC2 instance types documentation
.
Implementation steps
Gather workload system
            requirements:
Document the workload's technical
            profile, including operating system, CPU and GPU core
            counts, system memory, storage type and capacity, network
            bandwidth, and any required processor type. Record the
            source for each figure so reviewers can judge its
            reliability.
Identify the constraining
            dimension:
Analyze the requirements together to
            find which dimension limits the workload, rather than
            reacting to the most visible one. Use this to select the
            resource family, such as general purpose, compute optimized,
            memory optimized, storage optimized, or accelerated
            computing.
Select type and size from
            data:
Use your cost model and workload data to
            choose a specific type and size within the family, setting
            virtual CPU count, memory, local and
Amazon EBS
storage, and network performance to match the
            required data transfer rate. Estimate the number of
            resources needed for the anticipated load.
Prefer purpose-built resources for
            stable profiles:
When a
purpose-built processor or instance type
matches a well-understood
            workload, select it over a general-purpose equivalent for
            better price performance. Keep general purpose where the
            profile is uncertain or likely to change.
Validate against cost and
            performance:
Confirm the selection against the
            cost model and, where possible, a benchmark under predicted
            load. Adjust the type, size, or number if measured behavior
            differs from the source data.
